newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Euro growth stocks bourse Easdaq in listings drive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Euro growth stocks bourse Easdaq in listings drive.

text.p: Easdaq, the new market for European growth stocks, has embarked on a drive to get more listings in order to boost liquidity on the fledgling exchange.
"We want to reach a critical mass of 200 companies, then we will be okay," Jacques Putzeys, chief executive officer of the Brussels-based exchange told Reuters.

The European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation (Easdaq) is presenting its services at a series of roadshows this month in Milan, Amsterdam, Stuttgart, Rome, Lausanne, Frankfurt and London (dates on www.easdaq.be).
Easdaq, which started trading on November 27, currently has eight listings. Putzeys confirmed that listing requests for another six companies had been approved, while two others were in the pipeline.

"The good news is that before the summer break, we will double the number of companies listed," he said. He added that he hoped to have about 35 companies listed by the end of 1997, scaling down earlier hopes for 50 listings by then.

With a total market capitalisation of just $1.28 billion and average daily turnover of $1.3 million, Easdaq is small even compared to a small European exchange like the Brussels bourse, which has capitalisation of $130 billion and average daily volume of $122 million.
A comparison with its big brother Nasdaq -- which is one of Easdaq's shareholders and the model for its European equivalent -- makes Easdaq look minute.
Nasdaq has 5,540 domestic and foreign listed companies, total capitalisation of $1.5 trillion (end of April) and average daily turnover of $16.3 billion (www.nasdaq.com).
"Nasdaq too has taken its time to grow, I think it will take Easdaq less time," said Pieter Hofman, head trader at Kredietbank Securities, one of Easdaq's market makers.

But although Easdaq is eager to grow, it vows to be selective. "It is very tempting to accept a lot of companies, but we have refused more companies than we have accepted so far, in the long run, quality is very important," Putzeys said.
DIFFERENT FROM EURO.NM, AIM
Easdaq wants to list young, high-tech companies with a European calling. EASDAQ EAS01

Its first listings have fit that bill, such as the British anti-virus software firm Dr Solomon's Group, the Belgian biotechnology firm Innogenetics, the Belgian pre-press software firm Artwork Systems, the French computer security firm ActivCard, U.S. flat panel display maker PixTech, British telecom group Esprit Telecom and French microbiology testing firm Chemunex.
The Swiss paper and pulp group Mercer International is the only Easdaq-listed firm in a traditional industry.
"We want high-tech companies. We would not look at property companies. And if a company has no European aspirations, it is better off in a national market," Putzeys said.
He added that he saw no competition between Easdaq and the small-cap bourses set up by national bourses such as Euro.NM.
"We are completely different from the Euro.NM. We offer a pan-European trading platform, the Euro.NM markets are not linked yet," Putzeys said.

Euro.NM ("New Market") -- which also sees Nasdaq as a role model -- wants to create a common technological platform for trading small-company stocks between the Paris, Brussels, Amsterdam and Frankfurt bourses.
The Paris Nouveau Marche was launched in February 1996, the other NM markets were launched earlier this year.
The London-based Alternative Investment Market (AIM) has attracted more than 250 companies since its launch in 1995.
"AIM profiles itself as a national market, they are also less regulated than we are and do not have the same transparency requirements," Putzeys said.
Kredietbank Securities' Hofman said that the main advantage of Easdaq over national markets was that on Easdaq it would be easier to compare companies within the same business sector.
"If a Finnish biotech company wants to go public, it would be better of on Easdaq than on the Helsinki bourse," he said.
However, Easdaq's focus on young, growth companies also makes it miss promising listings.

Belgian Hamon, a world leader in cooling systems for power plant, will go public on the Brussels bourse's cash market in June. A heavyweight high-tech group like Hamon could have given a strong boost to Easdaq's capitalisation and liquidity.
"We have seriously considered Easdaq. But it really is more a market for start-up companies," Hamon chief executive Francis Lambilliotte told Reuters.
EDUCATING EUROPE ABOUT QUARTERLY REPORTING
Putzeys said that what sets Easdaq apart -- besides the techno-bent -- is its adherence to strict, Nasdaq-style accounting and reporting standards.
Most notable is the requirement that its listed companies report quarterly earnings, a requirement most blue-chip European bourse do not even impose.

Easdaq also requires its companies to present their financial information in accordance with International Accounting Standards (IAS) or United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (US GAAP).

Home country accounting standards are accepted, but in that case, the difference between these standards and IAS or US GAAP must be stated and any figure that would differ must be detailed under one of the two standards.
With the exception of Chemunex, all Easdaq companies so far have chosen the more prescriptive GAAP standards.
"We bring Nasdaq standards to Europe. If companies prove that they can comply with them, the next step, in a few years, is a listing on Nasdaq itself," Putzeys said.
A QUOTE-DRIVEN MARKET
He added that the strict reporting requirements were inherently linked to Easdaq's trading system, in which market makers take positions in the shares for which they advertise bid and ask quotes.
"You cannot make a market in a share if you have no information for six or nine months. In an order-driven market, the middle man always has an order behind him," Putzeys said.
Easdaq is essentially a telephone market. Screens are used to post prices and report transactions, but the actual deal is made on the phone.

Easdaq's screen system is the International Securities Market Asssociation's (ISMA) Trax, a Eurobond trading system which has been adapted for equities. It has a link with the Swiss-based settlement agency Intersettle. ($1 = 35.65 Belgian francs)
